home_spot.short_description_plain_text: The crisis in psychiatry wasn't a sudden accident; it’s a "looping effect" that has been rewriting human nature for decades. While we've been focused on the biology we can see, the reality of the human mind is that we are being shaped by classifications we often mistake for discoveries. We are effectively trying to treat the soul while wearing a biological blindfold. From the "epidemic" of Multiple Personalities in the 90s to the day Homosexuality was simply voted out of existence by the DSM in 1973, the way we label human suffering is changing how we live. How did we end up in a global scramble to treat disorders that might be partly created by the very manuals used to diagnose them, and what does the "new map" of the human mind look like from the perspective of its most misunderstood behaviors?The Session:Dr. Shinod N.K. joins us to dissect the mechanics of Dynamic Nominalism - the philosophical reality that naming a condition actually changes the person being named. Moving from the rigid, objective laws of Physics to the fluid epistemology of the mind, Shinod brings a rare perspective on how 50 years of shifting classifications are finally catching up with us. This isn't a therapy session; it’s a masterclass in Ontological Mystery and Conceptual Survival. Missing this means missing the chance to understand the very labels that define our modern lives.What to Expect:50-minute Masterclass: On "The Looping Effect," the shifting status of the DSM, and why the global "Science Map" of the mind is being redrawn by committees rather than microscopes.15–20 mins Q&A: Challenge Shinod on the "Brain-First" myth, the politics of psychiatric labels, and the reality of "inventing" disorders in 2026.30-minute Mixer: Discuss the new "mental world order" and the ethics of diagnosis with fellow skeptics at Windmills.One complimentary mocktail included.Event Details:📅 Date: 03/05/26 | 4 PM – 6 PM📍 Venue: Windmills, Hyderabad (Madhapur)🎫 Limited seating available💰 Early bird pricing for the first 20 tickets.About the Lecturer:Dr. Shinod N.K. is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at the University of Hyderabad and a former Post-Doc Research Affiliate at IIT Delhi. A Gold Medalist in M.Phil (Pondicherry University), he specializes in the History and Philosophy of Science. Having transitioned from a background in Physics to the complex epistemology of psychiatry, his work focuses on the boundaries where scientific data meets human narrative. In his downtime, he is a published poet and a fan of philosophical cinema.About Pint of View:Inspired by Lectures on Tap (U.S.), we’re bringing big ideas to the table in Hyderabad. No whiteboards, no exams—just high-level intellect served with a side of irony.

home_spot.short_description_plain_text: 🧠 The Brain Bar presents“Your Closet Is Full. So Why Is Getting Dressed So Hard?”📅 Saturday, May 2nd | 🕔 5:00 PM – 7:00 PM📍 3 Bears Cafe, Financial District If we have more clothing choices than any generation before us, why do so many of us feel worse getting dressed?Closets are fuller. Trends move faster. Style advice is everywhere.And yet every morning, people still stand in front of wardrobes feeling unsure, underwhelmed, or strangely disconnected from what they wear.Too plain. Too much. Too old. Too forced. Too expensive to fix.So what’s really going on?About the Session:Fashion is rarely just about clothes. It shapes first impressions, confidence, identity, belonging, gender expectations, status, and the quiet fear of being judged.This session explores why getting dressed has become unexpectedly complicated in modern life and why having more options often creates more confusion, not more freedom.We’ll unpack questions like:Why do people with full wardrobes still feel like they have nothing to wear?Who created the “rules” of dressing well and who benefits from them?Why does fashion advice often feel aspirational but unusable?Why do trends make us buy more, yet feel less satisfied?Why do many men feel excluded from style conversations until they need help?Why has the best fashion advice in your life probably come from a woman?What does it truly mean to develop personal style instead of performing one?We’ll also look at how clothing has evolved from utility to identity marker and how culture, media, and insecurity now shape what hangs in our closets.This is not a lecture on brands or aesthetics.It is a sharp, honest conversation about why something as ordinary as getting dressed can feel so psychologically loaded.Some of it may sting. But it may also change how you look at your wardrobe forever.About the Speaker:Prof. Jasti Pooja is an Associate Professor in the Department of Fashion Design at National Institute of Fashion Technology. An alumna of National Institute of Fashion Technology and National Institute of Design, she brings both industry and academic experience to her work in fashion education. Her teaching and research focus on pattern making, fashion theory, and the history of fashion, exploring how design, culture, and craft intersect. Since joining NIFT in 2009, she has also served as Course Coordinator in the Fashion Design department, helping shape the next generation of designers.About The Brain Bar:The Brain Bar is a series of intimate, idea-driven gatherings hosted in cafés and bars, where complex ideas are explored through engaging, discussion-led conversations. It’s where you come not just to listen, but to think, question, and see the world a little differently.If you’ve ever looked at a full closet and still felt like you had nothing to wear - this conversation is for you.

home_spot.name: A Quiet Morning
home_spot.short_description_plain_text: A Quiet Morning is a 90-minute sensory experience designed for those who need a genuine reset. Set in the lush, plant-filled surroundings of Urban Nemo Cafe & Garden in Jubilee Hills, this is a morning that moves through you slowly, intentionally, and without agenda.What the morning holdsYou'll be guided through four experiences, each building on the last.It begins with Shinrin Yoku, a forest bathing meditation — a Japanese practice of sensory immersion that settles the mind. A gentle functional mobility flow follows, accessible to all bodies and all ages, to awaken the body. Djembe beats take slowly. A single heartbeat. Slow, low, and deliberate, until the whole room is breathing with it. The morning closes with a sharing circle — one word each, offered to the room.Breakfast at Urban Nemo follows — coffee or fresh juice, a fruit bowl, and open toast. Included with your ticket.This is not a yoga class. It is not a workshop. There is nothing to learn and nothing to perform. Limited seats. One morning. Nothing to bring but yourself and a mat.
